clue.text: Lord, a boy fortunately hurt only a single time

indicators.note: hurt means damaged or injured, so the letters of the word before it are knocked into a new order
only a single says that of the two of these letters in the word just one is kept

explanation.surface: A lord recalls that, luckily, a boy was injured just once.
explanation.walkthrough: FORTUNATELY has two Ts; 'only a single time' drops one to leave FORUNATELY, which 'hurt' rearranges. Little Lord Fauntleroy is the boy hero of Frances Hodgson Burnett's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Lord Fauntleroy, the title character of the Burnett novel, is a young boy who becomes heir to an earldom.

clue.text: If orator fails, I can follow with more reason

indicators.note: fails suggests something breaking down, so the letters of the preceding words collapse and are rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A speaker admits that if the orator flops, he can step in afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails' looks like the verb of the surface, but it is the anagram signal; 'can follow' places the lone I at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortiori is a Latin phrase used in argument meaning from a stronger reason, so all the more so.

clue.text: It has China to the north-east

definitions.text: It has China to the north-east

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation for north-east
china is rhyming slang for mate (china plate), so a pal

explanation.surface: A geography question about which country sits with China lying above it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate = mate), not the country; in a down entry the compass piece sits above the friend, to its north.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan kingdom of Nepal borders Tibet, part of China, along its whole northern frontier.

clue.text: In resort, girl introduces friend to mum

indicators.note: introduces means brings in, so the girl takes the following pieces into her middle

parts.note: lass is a word for a girl
a pal is a friend
ma is an informal word for mum

explanation.surface: On holiday at a resort, a girl introduces her friend to her mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introduces' puts friend and mum together inside the girl. Las Palmas is the main city and resort of Gran Canaria.
explanation.definitionFit: Las Palmas, on Gran Canaria, is a popular holiday resort in the Canary Islands.

clue.text: Valuable coin that's on Welsh table?

parts.note: something rare is precious and valuable
a bit is a small coin, as in a threepenny bit

explanation.surface: A precious coin is set out on a table in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: A threepenny bit was an old British coin. Welsh rarebit is cheese on toast, served at a Welsh table; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rarebit is the toasted cheese dish, so it is food you might find laid on a table in Wales.

clue.text: Produce my Times, lad, regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of these words is taken

explanation.surface: A lad is told to bring forth copies of the newspaper on a routine basis.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th and 10th letters of MY TIMES LAD.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to produce, as a field yields or produces a crop.

clue.text: Chapter header: "Dare to sample drug"

indicators.note: to sample means to take a taste, so the first piece takes the second into itself

parts.note: Dan Dare is the space pilot of the Eagle comic, so Dare leads to his first name Dan
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: An opening heading of a book urges someone to be brave and try narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: Dan Dare was the hero of the British boys' comic Eagle, so 'Dare' gives DAN, which 'to sample' sets around E.
explanation.definitionFit: A dean is the head of a cathedral chapter, the body of clergy who run it.

clue.text: One grows wild: instrument is in — please buy!

indicators.note: is in says the instrument sits inside the following phrase

parts.note: please buy is an urging to do get
the viol is an old stringed instrument

explanation.surface: A shop assistant urges a customer to buy a newly arrived instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'please buy!' is read as DO GET!, and 'is in' places VIOL inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The dog violet is a scentless wild violet common in hedgerows and woodland.

clue.text: Shaw found among hearties?

indicators.note: found among says the letters wanted lie within the word that follows

explanation.surface: A question whether the playwright Shaw was discovered among hearty folk.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw here is not George Bernard but the jazz clarinettist and bandleader Artie Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Artie Shaw was the American swing clarinettist and big-band leader, so the first name pairs with that surname.

clue.text: Councillor secures order to ask one to make notes

indicators.note: secures means holds tight, so the councillor's letters close around the rest

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit
to pose a question is to ask it

explanation.surface: A councillor obtains an order requiring someone to take minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make notes' suggests jotting things down, but the notes are musical.
explanation.definitionFit: A composer writes music, so is someone who produces notes.

clue.text: Opener misses out on heavy scores

indicators.note: the opener of the word is its first letter, which misses out, so it is dropped

parts.note: weighty means heavy

explanation.surface: A cricket opening batsman fails to make big totals.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of an opener missing out is a red herring; 'scores' as a plural number means multiples of twenty.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighty is four score, a score being twenty, so it is a number made of several scores.

clue.text: Swift favourite holders of money backed when weight dropped

indicators.note: dropped means let fall, so the weight's letter is taken out
backed means turned round, so the word for the holders is read in reverse

parts.note: wallets hold money

explanation.surface: A fast-running favourite gets backing in the betting while its handicap is lowered.
explanation.walkthrough: WALLETS 'backed' gives STELLAW, and 'when weight dropped' removes the W. The racing surface hides the satirist Jonathan Swift.
explanation.definitionFit: Stella was Jonathan Swift's name for Esther Johnson, his close companion and correspondent.

clue.text: Daughter's note, written in inner room, that's changed after guest leaves

indicators.note: written in says the following letters are put inside the room's word

parts.note: ben is the Scots word for the inner room of a cottage, as in but and ben
D is the abbreviation for daughter
a line is a short written note, as in drop me a line

explanation.surface: A daughter's letter, kept in a back room, is altered once a visitor departs.
explanation.walkthrough: BEN is the inner room of a two-roomed Scottish cottage (the outer is the but). 'note' is a written note, not a musical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheets and pillowcases are what a host strips and changes once a visiting guest has gone home.

clue.text: Say: Clare, darling, accept love!

indicators.note: accept means take in, so the term of endearment holds the next letter

parts.note: pet is a term of endearment like darling
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone named Clare is addressed fondly and urged to take love on board.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare is not a woman but John Clare, the English peasant poet; 'Say' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: John Clare was the nineteenth-century Northamptonshire poet, so he is an example of a writer of verse.

clue.text: Empty out, with the rest, alloy used by printers

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: et al, short for et alii, means and the rest

explanation.surface: Someone is told to empty everything, along with the rest, of a printer's alloy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges EMPTY as TYPEM; 'with' joins ET AL, the Latin abbreviation for 'and the rest'.
explanation.definitionFit: Type metal is the alloy of lead, tin and antimony from which printing type was cast.

clue.text: Faced having to cancel mass for husband — it's what keeps him going

parts.note: met means faced, as in met a challenge

indicators.note: mass for husband means the letter for mass takes the place of the letter for husband

parts.note: to abolish is to cancel

explanation.surface: A man faced the scrapping of something, which is what keeps him motivated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps the letter for husband with the one for mass. 'him' is any living body, not the husband of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Metabolism is the chemical process that turns food into energy and keeps a body alive and active.

clue.text: Cracking monster secret code, soldier finally gets decoration at the front

indicators.note: cracking means breaking into, so the next letter splits the monster's word

parts.note: a beast is a monster

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word soldier

parts.note: a PIN is a personal identification number, a secret code

explanation.surface: A soldier breaks a fearsome secret cipher and is decorated on the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' sets the last letter of 'soldier' inside the monster. 'at the front' suggests the battlefield but means on the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: A breastpin is a brooch or ornamental pin worn on the chest, so a decoration worn at the front.

clue.text: Commendatore's perch?

parts.note: in Don Giovanni the Commendatore returns as a statue sung by a deep male voice; perch is also a fish, and a sea fish of that family has this name

explanation.walkthrough: In Mozart's Don Giovanni the murdered Commendatore comes back as a talking statue, a bass role; the answer is also a perch-like sea fish, the wreckfish.
explanation.definitionFit: The stone bass is a perch-like sea fish, and the phrase also describes the Commendatore's statue sung by a bass.

clue.text: Non-essential operations put back, cripple accepts

indicators.note: accepts means takes in, so the word for cripple holds the reversed piece

parts.note: to disable is to cripple

indicators.note: put back means turned round, so the abbreviation for operations is read backwards

parts.note: ops is short for operations

explanation.surface: Unimportant surgical procedures are postponed, and a disabled patient agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' hints at postponing surgery but reverses the operations' abbreviation, which 'accepts' places inside the word for cripple.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disposable can be thrown away, so it is dispensable and inessential.

clue.text: Napoleon admits medic is like hardline Tory

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so Napoleon's nickname takes the doctor inside

parts.note: Boney was the British nickname for Napoleon Bonaparte
DR is the abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: The French emperor lets in a doctor who is a right-wing Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links. A 'dry' in British politics was a hardline Thatcherite Conservative, opposed to the moderate 'wets'.
explanation.definitionFit: In UK politics a dry was a hardline Thatcherite Tory, so a totally dry one is uncompromising.

clue.text: Accepted as closed? Fine

parts.note: to means shut, as a door pulled to
OK means fine

explanation.surface: A question whether something was regarded as shut, answered with approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' as an adverb means closed, as in 'push the door to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Took is the past tense of take, which can mean accepted, as in took the offer.

clue.text: Finest poet captures hearts

indicators.note: captures means holds inside, so the poet's name encloses the card suit letter

parts.note: Thomas Campion was an Elizabethan poet and composer
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games

explanation.surface: The best poet wins people's affections.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Campion (1567-1620) wrote lute songs and poems; H for hearts is a bridge abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Champion as an adjective means first-rate or best, as in a champion effort.

clue.text: Strong desire to block cry of surprise — one may be spotted

indicators.note: to block means to stand in the middle and obstruct, so the desire goes inside the cry

parts.note: ha is an exclamation of surprise
a yen is a strong desire or longing

explanation.surface: An intense longing stifles a gasp, and the person might be noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spotted' reads as noticed, but it means having spots, as the spotted hyena does.
explanation.definitionFit: The spotted hyena is the best-known species of this African scavenger, its coat marked with dark spots.

clue.text: I raise soldiers to secure right against property

indicators.note: raise in a down entry means lift up, so the piece is read from bottom to top
to secure means to hold inside, so the soldiers enclose the letter for right

parts.note: men is a common word for soldiers

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of raising troops to win a legal right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to secure' puts R in MEN to make MERN, which 'raise' turns over to NREM after I.
explanation.definitionFit: In rem is a legal Latin term for an action or right directed against a thing or property, not a person.

clue.text: You find nothing in tiny piece I left

indicators.note: in says the nothing goes inside the trimmed word
left means departed, so the letter I goes out of the word

parts.note: a sliver is a tiny piece
taken as written
nothing is zero, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone discovers there is nothing inside a tiny fragment that was left over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I left' removes I from SLIVER (SLVER) and 'in' places O inside. 'You' means the person doing this crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: The reader tackling the puzzle is the one cracking the clues, so 'you' is the person working it out.

clue.text: One in bath is cold, dropping article to bottom

indicators.note: dropping to bottom means the article falls to the end of the word, which in a down entry is the bottom

parts.note: aloof means cold and distant
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone in the bath is chilly, and lets an item fall to the bottom of the tub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping ... to bottom' moves the A of ALOOF to the end. The bath picture makes 'cold' read as temperature, but it means unfriendly.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofah is a dried gourd used as a bath sponge, so it is an object found in the bath.

clue.text: Late evening sun is a pointer

definitions.meaning: a sun late in the evening is one that is going down below the horizon
a pointer is a gundog, and the related breed that crouches to show game is this one

explanation.surface: The sun sinking late in the evening points the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is a gundog that 'sets', crouching to indicate game, much as a pointer points; the sun 'sets' at evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinking sun is one that sets, and the setter is a gundog breed akin to the pointer.

clue.text: Our Man in Havana finally sold very cheap — look at cover

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of the word sold

parts.note: very cheap is 1p, a single penny, read as IP
lo is an old word for look
a mat is a cover, as for a table or floor

explanation.surface: Greene's spy novel, at the end, sold for a pittance, so look at the jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very cheap' is 1p, one penny, which reads as IP. 'Our man in' a capital is a stock phrase for a country's ambassador.
explanation.definitionFit: Our man in a foreign capital is the stock phrase for a country's envoy or ambassador there.

clue.text: Sounding fit in horrid weather

indicators.note: sounding says the word for fit is heard, not seen

parts.note: hale means fit and healthy, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: A person sounding healthy despite awful weather.
explanation.walkthrough: HALE and HAIL sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Hail, falling pellets of ice, is a nasty kind of weather.

clue.text: Anyone's aim can be wrong? Sauce!

indicators.note: can be wrong suggests a mistake, so the letters of the words before are disordered

parts.note: taken as written, its S included
taken as written

explanation.surface: Anybody might miss the target, and someone retorts cheekily.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the S of 'Anyone's' is part of the fodder. 'Sauce!' looks like an exclamation of cheek, but it is the dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayonnaise is a cold sauce of egg yolk, oil and vinegar.
